newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares end sharply lower on Sharon fears.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares end sharply lower on Sharon fears.

text.p: Israeli shares closed sharply lower on Tuesday as the market worried about the imminent appointment of Ariel Sharon as finance minister, traders said.
They added that the decline of U.S. shares on Monday had exacerbated the uncertainty, causing a much needed technical correction.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares ended down 2.32 percent, or 6.80 points, to 289.55 on all-share turnover of 188 million shekels against 229 million shekels on Monday.
The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 2.20 percent lower at 298.13.
"Sharon worries the market a lot," said Gad Hacker of Betucha Securities. "He's big spender who spends on ideology and doesn't believe in austere budgets or in liberal economic policy."
The former general is widely expected to get the finance portfolio in the next few days after the resignation of Dan Meridor last week.

"Sharon is not adding to investors' health because he is not in favour of fiscal tightening," said Ari Eidelhet of Zeller Eblagon Securities but said the trigger for today's decline was the slide of U.S. stocks.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average registered its second-largest point decline ever on Monday, finishing down 192.25 points to 7604.26.
"The market was only looking for a reason to decline. It has been ready for a correction for the past 10 days and since Sunday it has been trying to decline," Eidelhet said.
He added that a correction is seen as much needed step before the market can resume its rise.
Eyal Kolka of Sigma Securities said the market was concerned that the depreciation of the shekel that began at the end of last week was getting out of hand.
He said that if the currency continued to weaken and Sharon poses a threat to fiscal discipline, the Bank of Israel would hold or even raise interest rates.
The representative rate for the dollar was fixed on Tuesday at 3.5060 shekels against 3.4840 on Monday.
Kokla said he still believed the dominant factor in the market continued to be profit-taking on its earlier run-up and that the direction would change.
"There is a consensus in the market that the basic trend is still positive," he said.

"There's uncertainty. The market is nervous that perhaps the best is behind us," said Hacker, adding that he expected the atmosphere to remain nervous over the next several days. Nevertheless, he said the long-term outlook was still good.
Eidelhet added that the fact that volume was relatively low supports the feeling that the decline was only a technical correction.

The most active shares were Bank Leumi, which fell 2.5 percent at 555 agorot on turnover of 17.1 million shekels; Bank Hapoalim, which lost 0.25 percent to 770 agorot on volume of 11.5 million shekels; and Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, which fell 2.25 percent to 22,401 - Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
